sources.dependency_note: Narrative by Sir Henry Bunbury, who by his preface was then at the head of the Quartermaster-General's department of the British army in the Mediterranean and enjoyed the confidence of its successive commanders, and who by the narrative also had temporary charge of the Adjutant-General's department during the expedition to Calabria and rode the field at Maida. sources.document_date_note: A retrospective history by an author who died in 1831 (the Internet Archive's creator field), printed in this edition in 1856. The print year is not an event date.
sources.dependency_note: Retrospective history of the kingdom of Naples by Pietro Colletta, a Neapolitan officer whose own entry in this volume's index has him command the artillerymen in Capua and defend Castelnuovo (vol. I), and later explore Capri, address King Joachim, advise on the defence of Naples, serve as minister of war, and be imprisoned and taken to Bohemia (vol. II); the index gives him no role at Gaeta or Amantea in 1806, and the passages read do not establish one. It is a Neapolitan account, neither the Bourbon garrison's own record nor a French one. On Gaeta the author writes that 'amore delle armi proprie' (love of one's own arms) would prompt a description of every particular of the enterprise, a phrase the passages read do not explain. No source is named in the passages read.

sources.document_date_note: A 1913 translation of manuscript memoirs. By the unsigned account of the manuscripts that follows the introduction, the manuscript 'Memories of Naples between the years 1798 and 1806' was written during the author's two periods of retirement in Sicily, before his departure for Vienna; no exact date of writing is given. The print year is not an event date.
sources.dependency_note: Memoirs of Roger de Damas, who by them commanded the Neapolitan army corps sent to defend Calabria in 1806 and was beaten at Campo Tenese on 9 March 1806: side B's commander's own account, an interested and self-justifying one ('Listen to my story, and then judge me if you will'). By the unsigned account of the manuscripts that follows the introduction (the introduction is signed, in the OCR, 'LlSONCE PlNGAUD'), the manuscript of the Naples memories was written in Sicily before the author's departure for Vienna and is 'an absolutely contemporary document', and nothing was cut from the text of the first volume nor its style modified, though the usual spelling of proper names was restored; the author's own note says he wrote the manuscripts at his brother's request and left them to his children. The text is an English translation. The chapter notes are partly the author's (marked 'Author's note') and partly the editor's: for Campo Tenese the editor cites Duhesme's estimate of Rosenheim's corps, P. L. Courier's letter and Marulli's prisoner figure, and for the siege of Gaeta Mathieu Dumas, Koch's Mémoires de Masséna, vol. V, Du Casse and Gachot, so the editor's notes are not independent of those works. The author's narrative names no written source.

sources.dependency_note: Retrospective history of Masséna's campaigns by General Koch, written by its title page from the documents Masséna left and from those of the Dépôt de la guerre and the Dépôt des fortifications. It is the French side's account of the Army of Italy in 1805, written from its commander's papers and so an interested account. It prints French documents as pièces justificatives (the army's ordre de bataille of 18 October 1805, reports of Generals Duhesme and Molitor), so it is not independent of them. Austrian dispositions and strengths in it are second-hand. Angeli (1897) cites pages of this volume in his source notes for the actions at Verona, Caldiero, Pojano and Castelfranco (notes 52, 62, 63, 65, 66, 68, 76 and 95; page numbers read in the OCR), so Angeli is not independent of it for those actions.

sources.dependency_note: Retrospective history of Masséna's campaigns by General Koch, written by its title page from the documents Masséna left and from those of the Dépôt de la guerre and the Dépôt des fortifications. For the conquest of Naples in 1806 it is the French side's account, written from the papers of Masséna, who commanded the army that invaded the kingdom and, by Koch, the siege corps of Gaeta at its capitulation, and so an interested account. It prints documents as pièces justificatives, among them, in the passages read, the state of the troops employed at the blockade and siege of Gaeta and the articles of its capitulation, so it is not independent of them. Neapolitan, Sicilian and British strengths, dispositions and losses in it are second-hand: it gives the Gaeta garrison's strength in July 'd'après le rapport des déserteurs'. The passages read name no other narrative source for 1806. The editor's notes to Damas's memoirs (1913) cite this volume for the siege of Gaeta.
